# Problem 1

What is the correct way of installing a library in R?  

```{r, echo=T, eval=F}
A) install.packages("devtools")
B) install.packages(devtools)
C) library("devtools")
D) library(devtools)
```

## Answer
```{r, echo=T, eval=F}
A) install.packages("devtools")
```

## Explanation

**library** is used to call a package that already is installed, you can use the package name with **library** function without putting it in a string in case if it is already installed, but when installing a new package you need to provide the name of the package in a string.

# Problem 2

Do these two codes perform the same action ?

```{r, eval=F, echo=T}
a <- c(1:10)
a <- c(1,10)

A) TRUE
B) FALSE
```

## Answer 

B ) FALSE

## Explanation
```{r}
print(c(1:10))

```

# Problem 3

**a)** Get the schedule for CSE 270,  
Pick all the correct options.

```{r, eval=F, echo=T}
A) class_schedules["CSE270"]
B) class_schedules[0]
C) class_schedules[1]
D) class_schedules$CSE_270
```

## Answer

```{r, echo=T, eval=F}
A) class_schedules["CSE270"]
C) class_schedules[1]
```

## Explanation

C ) is wrong as indexing starts from 1 in R.  
D ) is wrong as for vectors $ opreator is not available.

# Problem 3

**b)** Get the schedule for all classes except ***CSE 270***,  
Pick all the correct options.

```{r, eval=F, echo=T}
A) class_schedules[-c("CSE270")]
B) class_schedules[2:4]
C) class_schedules[c(2,4)]
D) class_schedules[names(class_schedules) != "CSE270"]
```


## Answer

```{r, echo=T, eval=F}
B) class_schedules[2:4]
D) class_schedules[names(class_schedules) != "CSE270"]
```

## Explanation 

A ) is wrong as its used for dataframes and is not working for vectors.  
C ) is wrong as it will select only the second and fourth classes.

# Problem 4

Which of these code chunks will create a 3x3 matrix  
and fill it with numbers from 1 to 9.  
It should look like this.

```{r, eval=F, echo=T}
A) one_to_nine <- matrix(1:9)
B) one_to_nine <- matrix(1:9, byrow=TRUE, nrow=3)
C) one_to_nine <- matrix(c(1,9), byrow=TRUE, nrow=3)
D) one_to_nine <- matrix(rbind(c(1:3), c(4:6), c(7:9)))
```


## Answer

```{r, eval=T, include=FALSE}
one_to_nine <- matrix(1:9, byrow=TRUE, nrow=3)
```

```{r, eval=F, echo=T}
C) one_to_nine <- matrix(c(1,9), byrow=TRUE, nrow=3)
```

## Explanation
If you do not specify the attributes **byrow** and **nrow**, the function matrix will create a 1 x n dimensional matrix where n is the number of elements in your provided vector, even if you provide a vector that is not one dimensional, like in D ) .

## Answer

**a)** Write down the commands to change the column names and row names of   
the matrix ***one_to_nine***, set the column names to ("Lazio", "Roma" , "Juventus") and

# Problem 6

**a)** Write a code chunk to convert the matrix ***one_to_nine*** into a dataframe and name that dataframe
***standings_2020_2022***.

```{r}
# Option A
standings_2020_2022 <- as.data.frame(one_to_nine)
# Option B
standings_2020_2022 <- data.frame(one_to_nine)
```

# Problem 6

## Difference between data.frame and as.data.frame

data.frame() can be used to build a data frame while as.data.frame() can only be used to coerce other object to a data frame.

for example:
```{r, warning=F}
(df1 <- data.frame((1:9),1:3))
(df2 <- as.data.frame((1:9),1:3))
```

# Problem 6

**b)** Write a code chunk to add one more column to the data frame, name it "Napoli" and add values  
(4, 2, 3) for the values of that column.

```{r}
# Option A
standings_2020_2022$Napoli <- c(4,2,3)
# Option B (Creative one :D )
Napoli <- c(4,2,3)
standings_2020_2022 <- cbind(standings_2020_2022, Napoli)
# option C
standings <- cbind(standings_2020_2022, c(4,2,3))
colnames(standings) <- c(colnames(standings_2020_2022),  "Napoli")
```

```{r, eval=T, echo=F, include=F}
standings_2020_2022 <- as.data.frame(one_to_nine)
standings_2020_2022$Napoli <- c(4,2,3)
```

# Problem 7

**a)** R has a built in dataframe called ***iris*** that contains some information about Species.  
Write down the commands to get the data frame and show the last 3 observations of the data frame. 

```{r}
data(iris)
tail(iris,3)
```

**b)** Write a code chunk to create 2 new variables for the dataframe iris and call them ***Sepal.Area*** and ***Petal.Area*** and fill in the values with the area(width x length) of both variables correspondingly,

```{r, eval=T}
iris$Sepal.Area <- iris$Sepal.Length * iris$Sepal.Width
iris$Petal.Area <- iris$Petal.Length * iris$Petal.Width
```

# Problem 7

**c)** Write a code chunk to filter out the data frame ***iris*** to only include the species for which 
the variable ***Sepal.Area*** is greater than 10 and the variable ***Petal.Area*** is less than 1.

```{r, eval=T}
iris[iris$Sepal.Area > 10 & iris$Petal.Area < 1,]
```

# Problem 7 

**c)**

Using dplyr

```{r}
dplyr::filter(iris,(Sepal.Area > 10 & Petal.Area < 1))
```
